title: Air India Drops Delhi Baggage Re-Check as It Eyes New Australian Routes
excerpt: The carrier's Easy Connect service lets travellers from Australia clear customs and immigration at their final Indian destination instead of Delhi, cutting minimum connection times from three hours to 60 minutes — with 10 to 12 more cities set to join within six months.
body:
• Air India's "Easy Connect" service now lets passengers flying from Australia to Ahmedabad, Amritsar and Varanasi check baggage through to their final destination, clearing customs and immigration there instead of at Delhi airport.
  • Minimum connection time in Delhi falls from three hours to 60 minutes; 10 to 12 more cities — including Goa, Kochi, Guwahati, Pune and Kolkata — are expected to join the network within six months, pending Indian government approval.
  • Since the September launch, Air India's share of Melbourne–Amritsar traffic jumped from 32% to 55%, as travellers who previously routed through Southeast Asian hubs switch back to the Indian carrier.
  • What it means for you: if you fly Sydney or Melbourne to Amritsar, Ahmedabad or Varanasi on Air India, you no longer collect and re-check bags in Delhi — and through-checked fares can be booked on airindia.com, the app, or through your travel agent. If you fly to other Indian cities, wait before booking summer trips: the next batch of Easy Connect cities lands within six months.

Air India is scrapping one of the most dreaded rituals of flying into India — the Delhi baggage carousel — for passengers connecting beyond the capital. And it is using the goodwill from that fix to make a bigger play for Australian travellers.

Speaking in Melbourne this week, the airline's global head of sales, Manish Puri, said Air India's "Easy Connect" service now lets passengers from Australia check their bags through to Ahmedabad, Amritsar and Varanasi, clearing customs and immigration at their final destination rather than at Delhi. For eligible passengers, that means no baggage carousels, no re-checking luggage, and no immigration queue at Delhi before the domestic leg.

"We are allowed to now do a minimum connecting time because there is no work to be done at Delhi Airport," Puri said, speaking to Australian media including Karryon. "So you transit and connect within 60 minutes to four hours, any international flight."

The end of the Delhi shuffle

The change targets a pain point that had been costing Air India passengers. Almost 35% of travellers coming from Australia go beyond Delhi, and 12% travel beyond India altogether. Under the old process, they needed at least three hours of connecting time in Delhi — time spent collecting bags, re-checking them, and clearing customs and immigration mid-journey.

The same arrangement applies to return flights: passengers can check baggage all the way back to Australia and pass through border control at their original point of departure in India.

"This is a big game changer from Air India's perspective, but more importantly, from the customer's perspective, because a lot of travellers were avoiding coming into Delhi as a transit point."

— Manish Puri, Air India's global head of sales

The early numbers suggest passengers agree. On Melbourne–Amritsar, Air India's market share rose from 32% in September, when the hub-and-spoke service launched, to 55% — traffic Puri says the airline had previously been losing to Southeast Asian carriers flying into Amritsar and Hyderabad.

Why Australia is a strategic market

Puri called Australia "a very strategic market when we plan our network" — driven by its large Indian diaspora. Visiting friends and relatives traffic still accounts for almost 60% of Air India's Australian business, but the airline wants a broader mix: leisure travellers, students, and passengers transiting onward to Europe and the Far East.

The carrier has been backing that pitch with hardware. Air India now operates 11 weekly flights from Delhi to each of Melbourne and Sydney. Melbourne was upgauged to the larger B777, which carries more premium seats, and Sydney is due to get the refurbished 777-300ER product with 40 business class seats and eight first-class suites in the first quarter of next year.

That premium push is aimed at corporate travel, which Puri said accounts for about 10% of the airline's Australian business today but could rise to 25% with the new product. The airline's wide-body net promoter score has moved from minus 45 to between plus 37 and plus 40, while on Australian services it climbed from minus 28 to plus 16 after the new aircraft arrived.

What's next: more cities, maybe more routes

The Easy Connect network is still small — just Varanasi, Amritsar and Ahmedabad — but Puri expects "10 to 12 more cities" to be added within six months, pending government approval. The shortlist includes leisure destinations such as Goa, Kochi, Guwahati, Pune and Kolkata.

On the Australian side, speculation persists about Brisbane and Adelaide joining the network beyond the current 11 weekly Melbourne and Sydney frequencies. Puri would not confirm any new routes, but said the carrier would expand its global network in line with its fleet expansion and "would like to find more cities in this part of the world to add more destinations." Pressed on Perth and the soon-to-open Western Sydney International airport, he said "how and when the new cities will come is still not decided" — the initial priority is to densify the existing network, and the open-skies agreement means the airline needs no further permission to add capacity.

"India being almost in the middle of Europe and Australia, we knew that there is going to be a huge opportunity of going towards Europe and going towards Far East Asia and Australia."

— Manish Puri, Air India's global head of sales

That expansion depends on aircraft. Air India now flies about 177 aircraft, with low-cost arm Air India Express operating about 110, and has nearly 600 new aircraft on order. Wide-body deliveries have been slower than planned — Puri said the airline expected 25 by December 2025 but received zero — though the first line-fit 787-9 arrived in January and deliveries are expected to ramp to one aircraft a week from 2027. The airline says almost half its wide-body fleet is now new or refurbished, a figure it expects to reach 75% by the end of 2027.

Air India has also signed an MOU with India's Ministry of Tourism to co-brand with the revived Incredible India campaign — a sign that the hub-and-spoke strategy is as much about selling India as a destination as it is about fixing transit.
